summary: Shanghai fires gene-editing researchers after a child's death in a trial, a study suggests banned Nvidia chips trained top Chinese AI models, and Shenzhen locks down for APEC.
body: Shanghai has dismissed two lead researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's medical school and barred them from state science funding for five years, after a 6-year-old girl died in a first-of-its-kind trial that edited genes in the brain.[^1][^2] According to Chinese state media, citing a Shanghai task force, investigators found the team ignored warning signs from an animal safety study, left the death out of a published paper, and used a consent form that did not make the risk of death clear; they found no fabricated data.[^1] Shanghai is now inspecting other experimental gene and cell therapy trials, part of a national tightening that began in May.[^1]

In AI, a former OpenAI researcher who examined the published model files of DeepSeek, Moonshot and others found traces suggesting that DeepSeek V4 and Moonshot's Kimi K3 were trained on Nvidia Blackwell chips, which the US bans from export to China.[^3] TechCrunch notes this does not prove the law was broken, since training could have happened abroad, for example in Malaysia. Research group Epoch AI estimates about 2 million advanced chips reached China in 2024-25 through schemes that hid where they were going.[^3]

Daily life in Shenzhen, China's tech hub, is shaped this week by the APEC summit (leaders meet Nov 18-19). Drones are banned citywide until Nov 21, cars from outside the city are restricted in six districts from Nov 17, and police from across Guangdong have been drafted in; some residents told Radio Free Asia the security queues feel wasteful.[^4][^5] China's October data on retail sales, factory output and home prices comes out on Monday; forecasters expect retail sales growth to slow to about 0.8%.[^6][^7]

reads.title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China's most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
reads.summary: How researchers read clues in open AI models, what they suggest about banned chips in China, and the limits of that evidence.
